record_type_quote: Methods: Here we tested the replicability of these findings in a new cohort of news and press releases based on research in UK universities in 2014 and 2015.

targets.authors: Sumner P, Vivian-Griffiths S, Boivin J, et al.
targets.title: The association between exaggeration in health related science news and academic press releases: retrospective observational study.
targets.evidence_quote: The present study tested whether the findings of Sumner et al . (2014) , would replicate in news arising from UK university press releases in 2014 and 2015, using slightly improved methods (more even sampling and 100% double coding).
targets.outcome_quote: We found that the association between news and press releases did not replicate for advice exaggeration, while this association did replicate for causal claims and human inference from non-human studies. There was no evidence for higher news uptake for exaggerated press releases, consistent with previous results.
targets.outcome_reasoning: Authors explicitly distinguish replicated and non-replicated associations. The conclusion reinforces the main conclusions but also explicitly states advice was inconsistent; the general substantive picture is not an unqualified verdict that all replication comparisons agreed.

reasoning: New 2014/15 news and press-release sample directly retests Sumner 2014. Schat 2018 and other earlier replication attempts are contextual comparisons, not independent targets of this study. Reanalysis of original data described in discussion was done by Adams 2017 rather than this article.
